description.summary: The Lernaean Hydra is a many-headed serpentine drakōn of Greek mythology, offspring of Typhon and Echidna, slain by Heracles as his second labor; its defining trait is the regrowth of two heads for each one severed.
description.full: The Lernaean Hydra (Greek Λερναῖα Ὕδρα) is a chthonic, multi-headed serpent-monster of Greek mythology that lurked in the springs of Lerna in the Argolid, near a reputed entrance to the Underworld. Hesiod's Theogony names her parents as Typhon and Echidna and her siblings as Cerberus, Orthrus, and the Chimera. Sources differ on the number of heads — six on early bronze fibulae (c. 700 BCE), nine in Alcaeus, fifty in Simonides, and indeterminate in Euripides and Virgil — but the regenerating-head motif, first attested in Euripides, became canonical: each severed head sprouted two more (or three, in Servius). Heracles, sent against the Hydra by King Eurystheus as his second labor, ultimately defeated her with the help of his nephew Iolaus, who cauterized each neck stump with a firebrand to prevent regrowth. The single immortal head was severed and buried under a great rock between Lerna and Elaius. Heracles dipped his arrows in the Hydra's venomous blood, providing him a deadly resource for later labors and ultimately the means of his own death through the Tunic of Nessus. The Hydra became proverbial in Greek and remains a stock image for problems that multiply when attacked.

etymology.origin: Greek ὕδρα (húdra), 'water-snake', cognate with English 'otter' via the Indo-European root *wódr̥ ('water'). The name binds the creature to its watery lair at Lerna.
etymology.meaning: 'Water-snake of Lerna'; in classical usage 'Hydra' specifically denotes the Lernaean monster slain by Heracles.
etymology.first_use: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE) is the earliest extant narrative reference; the figure appears on Boeotian bronze fibulae of the same era.

features.description: Variously six (Boeotian bronze fibulae, c. 700 BCE), nine (Alcaeus, c. 600 BCE), fifty (Simonides), or indeterminate (Euripides, Virgil); nine became the canonical Renaissance figure
Each severed head regrows as two (or three, per Servius); first attested in Euripides
One head cannot be killed by any weapon and was finally buried under a great rock by Heracles
Even the scent of its breath was reputedly fatal; its blood served as the poison for Heracles's arrows
Long-bodied water-serpent form, sometimes shown with a double tail in archaic vase painting

physical.morphology: A polycephalous serpent-monster (drakōn) of chthonic class. Iconography from Boeotian fibulae (c. 700 BCE) and Caeretan black-figure hydriai (6th c. BCE) onward shows multiple sinuous necks rising from a single coiled body.

abilities.description: Two new heads grow in place of each one cut off; canonical motif from Euripides onward
Breath, scent, and blood are poisonous; remains so after death and provides Heracles's later arrow-toxin
Attacks from the spring of Amymone and the surrounding marshes of Lerna

behavior.diet: Cattle and human victims of the Argolid (in classical sources); functions in narrative as a chthonic guardian rather than a feeder
patterns: Lairs at the spring of Amymone
Emerges to ravage Lerna and surrounding lands
Functions as a guardian of a reputed underworld entrance

range.description: Mythological habitat is the marsh of Lerna, in the Argolid region of the Peloponnese, southern Greece, near a reputed entrance to the Underworld.

hotspots.name: Lake Lerna

location.description: Marsh and spring complex on the eastern coast of the Argolid Peninsula, near the modern village of Mýloi

hotspots.peak_period: Mythological; archaic to Classical Greek references
hotspots.notes: Historically a sacred site predating Mycenaean Argos, with the spring of Amymone (Pausanias, Description of Greece 2.37) as the Hydra's specific lair.

first_recorded.source: Boeotian bronze fibulae and Hesiod's Theogony

peak_activity_periods.description: Earliest narrative (Hesiod) and visual (bronze fibulae, Caeretan hydriai) attestations
Euripides establishes the regeneration motif; Plato uses the Hydra as a metaphor in the Euthydemus

peak_activity_periods.period: Hellenistic and Roman period, 3rd c. BCE – 5th c. CE
peak_activity_periods.description: Apollodorus, Ovid, Hyginus, Pausanias, Diodorus Siculus, and Servius transmit the canonical narrative

origins.cultural_roots: Belongs to the Greek tradition of chthonic monstrous offspring of Typhon and Echidna. The Hydra is one of a cluster of polycephalous serpents (Ladon, Cerberus, the Chimera) that guard liminal places.
origins.earliest_accounts: Earliest extant narrative is Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE), which gives the Hydra's parentage and the basic tradition. Boeotian bronze fibulae of the same era show a six-headed water-serpent attacked by a hero.
origins.folklore_connections: Comparable polycephalous serpents appear across Indo-European mythology (Ladon, Python, the Vedic Vṛtra) and beyond (Yamata no Orochi in Japan); the regenerating-heads motif is more specifically Greek.

timeline.event: Boeotian bronze fibulae depict a hero attacking a six-headed water-serpent, c. 700 BCE
timeline.significance: Earliest visual attestation of the Hydra tradition

timeline.event: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE) names the Hydra as offspring of Typhon and Echidna and sister of Cerberus and the Chimera
Alcaeus of Mytilene (c. 600 BCE) gives the Hydra nine heads
timeline.significance: Earliest specific head-count assignment in the canonical lineage

timeline.event: Euripides (5th c. BCE) attests the regenerating-heads motif
timeline.significance: First extant source for the iconic head-regrowth feature

timeline.event: Plato uses the Hydra as a logical metaphor in the Euthydemus (4th c. BCE)
timeline.significance: Early proverbial use of the Hydra for proliferating problems

timeline.event: Pseudo-Apollodorus's Bibliotheca (1st–2nd c. CE) gives the canonical Heracles-and-Iolaus account, including the immortal head buried under a rock
timeline.significance: Standard mythographic source for the second labor of Heracles

timeline.event: Pausanias's Description of Greece (2nd c. CE) locates the Hydra at the spring of Amymone
timeline.significance: Geographic anchoring of the myth in the Argolid

timeline.event: Servius (4th–5th c. CE) reports the variant of three heads regrowing per severance
timeline.significance: Late antique elaboration of the regeneration motif

timeline.event: Walter Burkert's Greek Religion published in English by Harvard University Press
timeline.significance: Standard modern reference framing the Hydra within Greek chthonic mythology

timeline.event: Daniel Ogden publishes Drakōn: Dragon Myth and Serpent Cult in the Greek and Roman Worlds (Oxford)
timeline.significance: Definitive modern study of Greek and Roman dragon-myth, including the Hydra

history.modern_era: The Lernaean Hydra remains a foundational image in Western culture: it gives its name to the constellation Hydra, to the genus Hydra of small freshwater cnidarians (so named by Linnaeus for their regenerative ability), and to the political idiom 'a hydra-headed problem'. It features extensively in modern fantasy from Dungeons & Dragons to Disney's Hercules (1997) and Marvel's HYDRA organization.

documentary.name: Hesiod, Theogony
documentary.description: Earliest extant Greek narrative naming the Hydra as offspring of Typhon and Echidna.
documentary.analysis: Foundational textual source for the Hydra's parentage and family of monsters.

documentary.name: Pseudo-Apollodorus, Bibliotheca
documentary.description: Standard mythographic narrative of Heracles's second labor, including Iolaus's cauterizing of the neck stumps and the immortal head buried under a rock.
documentary.analysis: Most influential surviving prose narrative of the labor.

documentary.name: Pausanias, Description of Greece
documentary.description: Topographical guide identifying the spring of Amymone at Lerna as the Hydra's lair.
documentary.analysis: Anchors the myth to a specific Argolid landscape.

documentary.name: Boeotian bronze fibulae
documentary.description: Bronze fibulae from Boeotia depicting a hero attacking a six-headed water-serpent.
documentary.analysis: Among the earliest visual attestations of the Hydra tradition.
documentary.source: Catalogued in Greek archaeological literature; cited in Ogden (2013)

scientific.name: Naturalistic rationalization
scientific.description: The 4th-century-BCE rationalist Heraclitus the Paradoxographer explained the Hydra as a single-headed snake accompanied by its offspring, which appeared multi-headed at a distance.

scientific.name: Geomythological reading
scientific.description: Some modern researchers (e.g. Luigi Piccardi 2005) have proposed that the Hydra myth encodes a memory of dangerous gas-emitting karst springs at Lerna, whose multiple vents and geothermal activity could anchor the polycephalous water-monster image.
evidence_cited: Karst hydrology of the Lerna basin
Co-occurrence of myth and geology in the Argolid

scientific.name: Comparative mythology
scientific.description: Modern scholarship situates the Hydra alongside Indo-European chaos-serpents (Vṛtra, Python, Ladon) slain by a hero-god, treating the regeneration motif as a literary intensification of the theme of difficulty.
evidence_cited: Iconographic continuity from archaic to Roman art

skeptical.name: Purely literary monster
skeptical.description: Mainstream classics treats the Hydra as a literary and religious figure of the Greek imagination with no historical referent; the 'evidence' is the Hesiodic and Hellenistic-Roman textual and iconographic record.
evidence_cited: Continuous attestation in poetry, drama, and art
Absence of any historical or biological claim in the ancient sources themselves

traditions: Argolid local tradition centered on Lerna
stories: The proverbial 'cutting off a hydra' (Plato, Euthydemus)
Hera placing the Hydra and the Crab in the night sky as the constellations Hydra and Cancer
folklore.beliefs: In ancient Greek religion, the Hydra is firmly mythological — a child of Typhon and Echidna belonging to the chthonic order subdued by Olympian heroes — rather than a creature of folk sighting tradition.
